**June 23, 1956 — A Saturday**

The summer of 1956 has a particular quality in retrospect: it was the last season in which Britain and France could still plausibly imagine themselves as world powers of the traditional kind. You were born into the final weeks of that illusion, on a day that was part of the mechanism of its unraveling.

---

**On the exact day you were born, Egypt voted**

Gamal Abdel Nasser stood as sole candidate in an Egyptian presidential plebiscite on June 23, 1956, ratifying a new constitution and his own authority with near-unanimous approval. The vote was formality dressed as democracy, but the moment was not trivial. Nasser was completing the consolidation of power that the 1952 coup had begun — ending Egypt's subordination to British influence, repositioning Egypt as the center of gravity for Arab nationalism, preparing for an act that would detonate the postwar international order. Thirty-three days later, on July 26, he nationalized the Suez Canal. Britain and France, joined by Israel, responded with military force in October. The United States — having decided the old empires were a Cold War liability — forced them to withdraw in humiliation. The world that existed before that sequence began is the world you were born into. The world that existed afterward is the one you grew up in.

---

**Eighteen days before your birth, a federal court ruled against segregation on buses**

On June 5, 1956 — eighteen days before you were born — a three-judge federal district court in Alabama ruled that bus segregation in Montgomery was unconstitutional. The ruling came as the boycott was entering its seventh month. The city appealed, and the buses remained segregated while the case worked its way upward. The boycott continued. The Black community of Montgomery kept walking, kept carpooling, kept sustaining their organized refusal into what would become the 381st day. The Supreme Court would ultimately affirm the lower court ruling in November. You were born seventeen days after a federal court established the legal principle; you were five months old when the highest court confirmed it and the boycott ended in victory. The civil rights movement's decisive early chapter was unfolding in the weeks immediately surrounding your birth.

---

**Earlier in June, physicists confirmed something Wolfgang Pauli had theorized in 1930**

In the early weeks of June 1956, Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan sent a telegram to Wolfgang Pauli informing him that they had detected the neutrino — the ghostly subatomic particle Pauli had proposed must exist a quarter century earlier, to account for apparent energy loss in certain radioactive decays. Pauli, who had despaired of the particle ever being found, responded with delight. The neutrino had been theorized to exist, provisionally named, and then hunted for twenty-six years. Its detection was a fundamental vindication of how theoretical physics worked — that mathematical reasoning about invisible things could be trusted, that the universe was coherent in the ways physicists supposed. You were born days after this confirmation arrived.

---

**The autumn that followed your birth would show what the thaw's limits were**

Khrushchev's February 1956 "Secret Speech" denouncing Stalin had opened a window of possibility across the Soviet bloc. In Poland, there was unrest and reform. In Hungary, reformers grew bolder through the summer and autumn. On October 23, 1956 — four months after your birth — students and workers took to the streets of Budapest. Soviet tanks entered Hungary on November 4 and crushed the revolution over ten days of fighting that killed thousands. The thaw had hard edges. The European order that had been imposed by Red Army occupation in 1945 would not be renegotiated by protest. That lesson was confirmed while you were a four-month-old infant, and it held until 1989.

---

**The arc of a lifetime**

You are 70.

The British Empire that Nasser was defying on the day you were born shed most of its remaining territory during your childhood and adolescence. You grew up in a world that was decolonizing — not tidily, not peacefully, but irreversibly. The countries that were colonies when you were born had, almost without exception, become independent nations by the time you were a teenager. The map of the world changed more rapidly in your lifetime than at any comparable period since the age of exploration.

You were five when Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth. Twelve when the Six-Day War reshaped the Middle East that Nasser had tried to lead. Thirteen when Apollo 11 landed on the moon. You grew up into Watergate and the oil shock and the end of the postwar economic boom. You were twenty-three when the Iranian Revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan announced that the 1970s' disorder would not resolve neatly. Thirty-three when the Berlin Wall fell and the Cold War — which had defined the entire world you were born into — ended with a startling absence of catastrophe.

The neutrinos confirmed just before your birth pass through your body at the rate of trillions per second, as they have every second of your life. They pass through everything without interacting, unseen and unimpeded. The physicists who announced their detection in June 1956 could not have known how much of physics, and how much of everything else, those invisible particles would eventually illuminate.

---

**What kind of world**

A Saturday in late June 1956 was the edge of something. The imperial structures that had organized global politics for a century were failing. The segregation that had organized American domestic life for nearly a century was losing its legal foundations. The atomic certainties of the early Cold War were giving way to thermonuclear uncertainties. A new generation was beginning — the one that would produce Elvis and the Beatles and everything that followed — though rock and roll in June 1956 was still new enough that serious people expected it to pass.

The people around your cradle had survived the Depression and the war. Some had fought. Some had rationed. All had reasons to hope that the grinding crises were finally past and that the prosperity now visibly spreading in American suburbs and gradually in European cities was the new permanent condition.

It was not permanent. But it was real, and it was yours for a while.
